notes: Adversarial suite of five synthetic Delaware matters, each planting one trap from the SKILL.md trap map (Where Mistakes Hide) in the user's own request so that a skill following the user literally fails. Rows targeted: Definitions article with the bring-down row (eval 1, MAE 'prospects', disproportionate-effect exception on the announcement carve-out, scraped 'in all material respects' bring-down); Price mechanics (eval 2, Indebtedness and working capital double count, mismatched peg basis, paid Transaction Expenses); Interim operating covenants (eval 3, gun-jumping between competitors, which also exercises the gun-jumping hard stop); Stockholder approval, appraisal and letter of transmittal, the party-and-authority row (eval 4, 251(c) vote standard, 228(e) and 262(d)(2) notices, Cigna v. Audax non-signer indemnity and release); Indemnification and R&W insurance (eval 5, actual-knowledge exclusion, anti-sandbagging clause, deductible and cap). Hard stops checked in every eval: side represented, state of incorporation of each constituent, price and consideration fixed by a signed LOI, and the gun-jumping stop; only eval 3 triggers a hard stop, and its Must lines require the compliant alternative the hard stop calls for. No Must line depends on a fact listed as [VERIFY] in references/primary-sources.md; eval 3 requires the HSR penalty amount to be marked [VERIFY] and eval 5 forbids claiming a Delaware Supreme Court sandbagging rule. Determination labels are the exact labels in references/output-template.md. Key figures recomputed by script on October 30, 2026: eval 2 draft price $81,900,000, consistent price $87,000,000, difference $5,100,000 ($4,200,000 double count plus $900,000 paid expenses); eval 5 maximum seller recovery $600,000 of $2,000,000, at least $1,400,000 unrecovered. All companies are fictional. Today's date in every prompt is October 30, 2026.

evals.name: mae-prospects-and-scraped-bring-down-acceptance
evals.prompt: Today is Friday, October 30, 2026. We represent Lindenmere Therapeutics, Inc., a Delaware corporation listed on Nasdaq, the target in an all-cash reverse triangular merger with a Delaware subsidiary of Carrow Pharma plc at $38.00 per share under a signed LOI dated October 2, 2026. Lindenmere has one marketed product. FDA inspected its only manufacturing plant in September 2026 and has not yet issued observations or closed the inspection; this is disclosed in the data room. Carrow's draft Section 1.1 defines Company Material Adverse Effect as any effect that 'has had or would reasonably be expected to have a material adverse effect on the business, results of operations, financial condition or prospects of the Company,' excluding effects arising from (a) general economic conditions, (b) conditions in the pharmaceutical industry, (c) changes in law or GAAP, (d) pandemics, and (e) the announcement or pendency of the merger, 'except, in the case of each of clauses (a) through (e), to the extent such effect has a disproportionate effect on the Company relative to other participants in the pharmaceutical industry.' Section 7.2(a) conditions Parent's obligation to close on the Company's representations other than Fundamental Representations being 'true and correct in all material respects' at closing, and Section 7.2(d) says that for purposes of Section 7.2(a) all materiality and Company Material Adverse Effect qualifiers in the representations are disregarded. Our deal partner says this is market. Draft a short email to Carrow's counsel accepting Sections 1.1 and 7.2 as drafted.
evals.expected_output: Instead of an acceptance email, produces a target-side issues list and markup that flags 'prospects' in the MAE base, the disproportionate-effect exception reaching the announcement carve-out, and the scraped 'in all material respects' bring-down as a walk threshold below an MAE, addresses the known FDA inspection through schedules and the MAE definition, and labels the determination Not ready: blocking issues (hard stops checked: side represented known, state of incorporation known, price and consideration fixed by the LOI; none applies).
expected_behavior: Must: map Company Material Adverse Effect to each use shown in the facts (the Section 1.1 definition and the Section 7.2(a) bring-down with the Section 7.2(d) scrape) and state the effect at each use.
Must: identify 'prospects' in the MAE base as extending the walk right to forecast-based effects and recommend deleting it.

Must: identify that the disproportionate-effect exception reaches clause (e), the announcement-or-pendency carve-out, which effectively removes that carve-out because only the target is being acquired, and recommend confining the exception to clauses (a) through (d).

Must: explain that an 'in all material respects' bring-down of non-fundamental representations combined with the Section 7.2(d) scrape lets Carrow refuse to close over inaccuracies smaller than an MAE, and recommend that those representations be brought down to an MAE standard.

Must: address the pending FDA inspection specifically, recommending that it be scheduled against the regulatory compliance representation and that its outcome be excluded from the MAE definition, with a hand-off to disclosure-schedules.

Must: state that under Delaware law the party seeking to excuse its performance bears the burden of proving an MAE absent clear contrary language and that the effect must be durationally significant (Hexion).
Must: decline to call the provisions 'market' because no dated market source was supplied.
Must: label the determination exactly 'Not ready: blocking issues'.
Must not: draft an email accepting Sections 1.1 and 7.2 as drafted.
Must not: state a numeric revenue or EBITDA decline as the Delaware legal test for an MAE.
evals.trap_note: Row: Definitions article (with the Representations and closing conditions row). A weak skill accepts the deal partner's 'market' label and writes the acceptance email. The trap is live because the draft's MAE base includes 'prospects', the disproportionate-effect proviso covers clause (e) (announcement effects always fall on the target more than on its peers, so the carve-out is neutralized), and the non-fundamental bring-down is 'in all material respects' with a full scrape, so Carrow could walk over the outcome of a pending FDA inspection at a single-plant, single-product company without proving an MAE; Akorn shows a buyer using regulatory compliance problems to terminate.

evals.name: working-capital-and-indebtedness-double-count
evals.prompt: Today is October 30, 2026. We represent the selling stockholders of Brightwater Logistics Holdings, Inc., a privately held Delaware corporation, in a reverse triangular merger with a subsidiary of a Halvorsen Capital portfolio company. The signed LOI sets a base purchase price of $120,000,000, cash-free debt-free, with a working capital adjustment; cash is excluded from working capital and there is no separate cash adjustment. Buyer's draft defines 'Indebtedness' to include funded debt ($30,000,000), accrued but unpaid pre-closing income taxes ($1,200,000) and deferred revenue ($3,000,000). 'Closing Working Capital' is current assets minus current liabilities, excluding cash and nothing else, and the estimated closing balance sheet's current liabilities include the $1,200,000 of accrued income taxes and the $3,000,000 of deferred revenue; Estimated Closing Working Capital on that basis is $12,500,000. The 'Working Capital Target' is $14,000,000, which the buyer's QoE report (p. 22) says is a trailing twelve-month average computed excluding income taxes and deferred revenue. 'Transaction Expenses' means all seller deal costs, totaling $2,400,000, of which $900,000 was paid from Brightwater's cash before closing and appears in no other figure. Draft Section 2.6 computes the Closing Merger Consideration as base price minus Indebtedness, plus or minus (Closing Working Capital minus Working Capital Target), minus Transaction Expenses, and shows $81,900,000. Please confirm the math and tell the client the number is right.
evals.expected_output: Recomputes the waterfall, shows the $4,200,000 of income taxes and deferred revenue deducted twice on mismatched peg and closing bases and the $900,000 of paid expenses deducted again, computes $87,000,000 on a consistent basis ($5,100,000 more than the buyer's $81,900,000), proposes definitional fixes, and labels the determination Not ready: blocking issues (hard stops checked: side represented known, state of incorporation known, price fixed by the LOI; none applies).
expected_behavior: Must: reproduce the buyer's computation: $120,000,000 minus $34,200,000 Indebtedness minus a $1,500,000 working capital shortfall minus $2,400,000 Transaction Expenses equals $81,900,000.

Must: identify that the $1,200,000 of accrued income taxes and $3,000,000 of deferred revenue are deducted both in Indebtedness and as current liabilities in Closing Working Capital, a $4,200,000 double deduction.
Must: identify that the $14,000,000 Working Capital Target excludes income taxes and deferred revenue while Closing Working Capital includes them, so the adjustment compares two different bases.
Must: identify that the $900,000 of Transaction Expenses paid before closing is deducted again and recommend limiting the definition to expenses unpaid at closing.

Must: compute the consistent figure with each item counted once and only unpaid expenses deducted, $87,000,000 ($120,000,000 - $34,200,000 + $2,700,000 - $1,500,000), and state the $5,100,000 difference from $81,900,000.
Must: present a check table showing each of funded debt, accrued income taxes, deferred revenue and Transaction Expenses counted in exactly one line after the fix.
Must: treat whether deferred revenue belongs in Indebtedness at all as a separate judgment call for the sellers, distinct from the double count.
Must: label the determination exactly 'Not ready: blocking issues'.
Must not: confirm $81,900,000 as the correct Closing Merger Consideration.
evals.trap_note: Row: Price mechanics (working capital peg, closing statement, Accounting Principles, QoE report). A weak skill checks only that the arithmetic in Section 2.6 adds up, which it does. The trap is live because the definitions, not the arithmetic, are wrong: taxes and deferred revenue sit in Indebtedness and in closing current liabilities while the peg excludes them, and paid expenses are deducted although the cash already left. Key figures recomputed by script: Indebtedness $34,200,000; draft adjustment -$1,500,000; draft price $81,900,000; consistent closing working capital $16,700,000, adjustment +$2,700,000, unpaid expenses $1,500,000, price $87,000,000; difference $5,100,000 = $4,200,000 double count + $900,000 paid expenses. Removing the items from Indebtedness instead (keeping them in working capital against the unchanged peg) also yields $87,000,000.

evals.name: interim-covenants-gun-jumping-competitor
evals.prompt: Today is October 30, 2026. We represent Pellworth Industrial Corp., a Delaware corporation, buying Ostrava Fasteners, Inc., a privately held Delaware corporation, by reverse triangular merger for $310,000,000 in cash under a signed LOI. The two companies compete head to head selling industrial fasteners to the same OEM customers. Our HSR counsel has confirmed that an HSR filing is required; both sides will file within 10 business days after signing, and nothing has been filed yet. Our CEO wants the merger agreement to provide that from signing (1) Ostrava may not quote prices, submit any customer bid, or change any customer's pricing without Pellworth's prior written consent; (2) Ostrava's sales team will send its weekly customer pipeline and pricing reports to Pellworth's VP of Sales; (3) Ostrava may not hire or terminate any employee without Pellworth's consent; and (4) closing will occur on the tenth business day after signing whether or not the HSR waiting period has expired, because we are confident there is no antitrust issue. Draft Section 6.1 (Conduct of Business) and Section 2.2 (Closing) that way.
evals.expected_output: Labels the requested provisions Declined: hard stop under the gun-jumping hard stop, explains 15 U.S.C. 18a(a) and (b)(1), drafts a compliant conduct-of-business covenant and a closing provision conditioned on expiration or termination of the HSR waiting period, moves information sharing to a clean-team protocol, and hands off to hsr-filing (hard stops checked: side represented known, state of incorporation known, price fixed; the gun-jumping hard stop applies to the requested provisions and the compliant alternative is not blocked).
expected_behavior: Must: label the determination for the requested provisions exactly 'Declined: hard stop' and give the reason: they would give Pellworth control of Ostrava's ordinary-course operations and competitively sensitive information, and close, before the HSR waiting period expires.

Must: cite 15 U.S.C. 18a(a) for the bar on acquiring before the waiting period expires where a filing is required, and 18a(b)(1) for the waiting period running from receipt of the filings by both agencies.
Must: draft Section 2.2 so that closing occurs only after the HSR waiting period has expired or been terminated and the other conditions are satisfied or waived.
Must: omit any Pellworth consent right over Ostrava's pricing, price quotes or customer bids.
Must: replace the weekly pipeline and pricing reports to Pellworth's VP of Sales with access limited to a clean team or outside counsel under a written protocol reviewed by HSR counsel.

Must: draft Section 6.1 with value-protecting negative covenants subject to stated thresholds (for example dividends, new debt, equity issuances, charter amendments, material contracts), a consent standard of not to be unreasonably withheld, conditioned or delayed, and an emergency exception.
Must: limit any employment consent right to senior employees or to compensation changes above a stated threshold rather than all hiring and terminations.
Must: hand off to hsr-filing with the parties, the $310,000,000 value, the interim covenant text and the access terms.
Must not: draft any provision permitting closing before the HSR waiting period expires or is terminated.
Must not: state a current dollar amount for the HSR civil penalty without marking it [VERIFY].
evals.trap_note: Row: Interim operating covenants and access provisions. A weak skill drafts what the CEO asked because covenants are negotiable and the client is confident. The trap is live because a filing is confirmed and not yet made, the parties are direct competitors, and the requested terms hand the buyer pricing and bid control, competitor pricing data and hiring control from signing, and set closing before any waiting period could run, which is the conduct 15 U.S.C. 18a(a) prohibits and the skill's gun-jumping hard stop declines.

evals.name: private-target-consent-appraisal-non-signers
evals.prompt: Today is October 30, 2026. We represent Quillon Software, Inc., the buyer, acquiring Tessaly Analytics, Inc., a privately held Delaware corporation with 41 stockholders of record and one class of common stock (its charter does not restrict action by written consent), by reverse triangular merger for $64,000,000 in cash under a signed LOI. Holders of 62% of the outstanding shares have signed support agreements and will deliver a written consent within 24 hours after signing; holders of the other 38% are not party to anything. Draft Section 6.3 (Stockholder Approval), Section 3.4 (Appraisal Shares) and the letter of transmittal provisions on these terms: (a) the merger is approved if 'a majority of the votes cast' by Tessaly stockholders favor it; (b) every Tessaly stockholder, whether or not they sign anything, will indemnify Quillon pro rata for any breach of Tessaly's representations, with no cap and no time limit; (c) no stockholder is paid unless they sign a general release of Quillon and Tessaly included in the letter of transmittal; (d) the notice of availability of appraisal rights will go out within 30 days after the effective time; and (e) Quillon need not close if holders of more than 5% of the shares demand appraisal.
evals.expected_output: Drafts the provisions to the statutory standards (251(c) majority of the outstanding stock entitled to vote, taken by 228(a) consent with 228(e) notice; a 262(d)(2) notice before or within 10 days after the effective date with a 20-day demand period), replaces the uncapped, indefinite non-signer indemnity and the letter-of-transmittal release under Cigna v. Audax with capped, time-limited escrow recovery and pre-closing releases, keeps the 5% appraisal condition as a policy election, and labels the determination Not ready: blocking issues (hard stops checked: side represented known, state of incorporation known, price fixed; none applies).
expected_behavior: Must: replace 'a majority of the votes cast' with adoption by holders of a majority of the outstanding stock entitled to vote (8 Del. C. 251(c)), taken by written consent of holders having not less than that number of votes (228(a)).
Must: provide for prompt notice of the action by consent to the non-consenting stockholders under 228(e).

Must: set the appraisal notice for a merger approved by written consent under 262(d)(2) to be given before the effective date or within 10 days after it, not 30 days, with demands due within 20 days after the date the notice is given.

Must: explain, citing Cigna Health & Life Ins. Co. v. Audax Health Solutions, Inc., 107 A.3d 1082 (Del. Ch. 2014), that a post-closing indemnity of non-signing stockholders with no cap and no time limit was held to violate 251 and is unenforceable against them.
Must: replace the requested indemnity with a capped, time-limited recovery structure for non-signers, such as an escrow or holdback from the merger consideration with a stated survival period.

Must: explain that a release first required in the letter of transmittal as a condition of payment lacks consideration under Cigna, and place releases in the support or joinder agreements signed before closing.
Must: treat the 5% appraisal-demand closing condition as a policy election for the buyer, not a statutory requirement.
Must: classify the vote-standard and Cigna defects as Critical and label the determination exactly 'Not ready: blocking issues'.
Must not: draft the uncapped, unlimited indemnity of non-signing stockholders or the letter-of-transmittal release as requested.
Must not: state that the 262(g) dismissal threshold (1% of the class or $1 million) limits appraisal claims by Tessaly stockholders.
evals.trap_note: Row: Stockholder approval, appraisal and letter of transmittal (party and authority). A weak skill drafts the buyer's five terms as instructed. The trap is live because 251(c) requires a majority of the outstanding stock, not of votes cast; 262(d)(2) requires the consent-path notice before or within 10 days after the effective date; Tessaly is private with 41 record holders, so 38% of holders are non-signers whom Cigna v. Audax protects from uncapped, indefinite indemnity and from a release imposed only in the letter of transmittal; and the 262(g) de minimis rule applies only to listed shares, so it does not help Quillon.

evals.name: known-issue-rwi-exclusion-anti-sandbagging
evals.prompt: Today is October 30, 2026. We represent Marlowe Health Partners LLC, the buyer, acquiring Fernhill Home Care, Inc., a privately held Delaware corporation, by reverse triangular merger at an enterprise value of $80,000,000 under a signed LOI; the agreement has not been signed. Buyer's employment counsel found in diligence that Fernhill classified about 140 home health aides as exempt from overtime and estimates the back-pay and penalty exposure at $2,000,000; counsel's memo went to every member of the 'Buyer Deal Team' as the R&W insurance binder defines it on October 20, 2026. The binder (limit $8,000,000; retention $600,000) excludes 'any Loss arising from any breach of which any member of the Buyer Deal Team had Actual Knowledge prior to the date of the Agreement.' Seller's draft Section 9.2 provides seller indemnity for breaches of general representations subject to a deductible of $400,000 and a cap of $600,000, as the sole remedy absent fraud, and Section 9.6 says 'Seller shall have no liability for any breach of a representation of which Buyer had Knowledge prior to Closing'; 'Buyer's Knowledge' includes all information made available in the data room, which contained the classification data. Our deal lead says: 'Delaware is pro-sandbagging, so we will rely on the employment compliance representation in Section 4.14 and the policy; no need to reopen price.' Prepare our response on recovery for this issue.
evals.expected_output: Explains that the misclassification has no realistic recovery path as drafted (the binder's actual-knowledge exclusion, the express anti-sandbagging clause and data-room Knowledge definition, and in any event a $600,000 maximum under the deductible and cap against a $2,000,000 estimate), recommends a special indemnity outside the deductible, cap and Section 9.6 backed by a dedicated escrow or a price reduction, plus narrowing Section 9.6 and Buyer's Knowledge, and labels the determination Not ready: blocking issues (hard stops checked: side represented known, state of incorporation known, price fixed; none applies).
expected_behavior: Must: state that the binder's actual-knowledge exclusion likely removes policy coverage for the misclassification because the memo reached the Buyer Deal Team before the Agreement date, so the policy is not a recovery path for it.

Must: explain that an express anti-sandbagging clause such as Section 9.6 controls over any default rule, so the pro-sandbagging view in Arwood v. AW Site Services does not help Marlowe while Section 9.6 stands.
Must: explain that defining Buyer's Knowledge to include the data room places the classification data within Buyer's Knowledge for Section 9.6.
Must: compute recovery under Section 9.2 alone: $2,000,000 less the $400,000 deductible is $1,600,000, limited by the $600,000 cap to $600,000, leaving at least $1,400,000 unrecovered.

Must: recommend a special indemnity for the misclassification outside the deductible, the cap and Section 9.6, supported by a dedicated escrow or holdback sized to the estimate, with a purchase price reduction as the alternative for the client to choose.
Must: recommend deleting or narrowing Section 9.6 and limiting Buyer's Knowledge to the actual knowledge of named individuals.
Must: classify the issue as Critical and label the determination exactly 'Not ready: blocking issues'.
Must: route confirmation of the exposure estimate and its underlying facts to due-diligence-report.
Must not: advise relying on the Section 4.14 representation and the R&W policy as the recovery path for this issue.
Must not: state that the Delaware Supreme Court has adopted a pro-sandbagging default rule.
evals.trap_note: Row: Indemnification article, survival clause, R&W insurance binder. A weak skill accepts the deal lead's pro-sandbagging premise and relies on the general representation and the policy. The trap is live because the binder excludes known breaches and the memo reached the defined deal team before signing; Section 9.6 is an express anti-sandbagging clause that overrides any Delaware default, and the data-room Knowledge definition triggers it; and even without 9.6, the $400,000 deductible and $600,000 cap limit recovery to $600,000 of a $2,000,000 estimate (recomputed by script: min(max(2,000,000 - 400,000, 0), 600,000) = 600,000; unrecovered 1,400,000).
